---
title: "Perceptual representations and efficient encoding"
description: "Representation learning, rate–distortion compression, and the perceptual prior as a mechanism for controlling coding complexity under partial observability."
toc-depth: 3
---

::: {#key-ideas .callout-note title="Key ideas"}
- Under limited processing capacity, a perceptual encoder must balance retaining
  distinctions useful for decisions against code complexity; minimizing
  complexity alone admits an uninformative channel.
- Temporal prediction and sensory reconstruction are candidate
  representation-learning objectives, but neither avoiding collapse nor
  achieving a good variational bound guarantees that the retained distinctions
  support good decisions.
- A learned normalized perceptual prior controls variational coding cost: for a
  fixed encoder and input distribution, improving the prior reduces prior
  mismatch in the coding bound without changing how much information the
  representations retain.
:::

In the [POMDP agent architecture](pomdp-rl.qmd#model-components), the
perceptual channel $F(z\mid x) = P(Z = z \mid X = x)$ determines which
distinctions in the sensory input $x$ reach the policy and memory update as a
latent $z$. If two observations call for different actions given the same
memory, mapping both to the same latent distribution leaves the policy unable to
respond differently. Conversely, biological code complexity is assumed to be
capacity-limited and costly: preserving every sensory detail expends capacity on
distinctions that never affect a decision.

Rate--distortion theory frames this trade-off between information retained and
errors introduced by compression [@sims2016]. Here, information rate serves as a
proposed surrogate for biological code complexity. Useful information must still
be enforced through a task-performance or distortion requirement; minimizing
complexity alone admits an uninformative channel.

## Representation learning

### Learning by temporal prediction

The predictive learning rule studied by @halvagal2023 works in latent space,
without reconstructing the sensory input. Predictive plasticity brings
representations of temporally adjacent inputs together, supporting invariance;
Hebbian plasticity preserves variation in activity and counters collapse.
Variation alone does not tell us whether the encoder distinguishes situations
that require different actions.

### Learning by reconstruction

A variational autoencoder adds a decoder $p_\psi(x\mid z)$. On inputs sampled
from a policy-induced input distribution $p(x)$, let expectations be under
$p(x)F(z\mid x)$. Following @alemi2018 [Eqs. 2--6], define reconstruction
distortion and variational coding cost by

$$
\mathcal D = \mathbb E[-\log p_\psi(X\mid Z)],\qquad
\mathcal C(F,\theta) = \mathbb E\!\left[\log\frac{F(Z\mid X)}{R_\theta(Z)}\right],
$$

where $R_\theta$ is a normalized perceptual prior. Jointly minimizing
$\mathcal D+\beta\mathcal C$ over encoder, decoder, and prior trades
reconstruction fidelity against coding cost for $\beta\geq0$; at $\beta=1$
the objective is the expected negative ELBO. The likelihood determines which
errors matter: a fixed-variance isotropic Gaussian gives squared error up to a
scale factor and a constant.

With well-defined entropy and log-loss, $H(X)-\mathcal D\leq I_F(X;Z)$.
Beating the best input-independent reconstruction loss therefore requires
informative latents. A good ELBO alone does not: an expressive decoder can
ignore $Z$, and positive coding cost can reflect prior mismatch rather than
retained information. Evaluate rate and distortion separately, then test whether
the policy can actually use the retained information on its task.

## Efficient encoding and the perceptual prior

### Perceptual prior

The learned model $R_\theta(z)$, also called the latent prior, describes which
perceptual representations are likely. In the first-version scope it captures
structure within a representation without predicting the next time step from
previous latents or actions: its parameters $\theta$ accumulate learning
experience, but temporal history is not an explicit input.

$R_\theta$ must be a normalized probability mass function or density, not an
arbitrary scalar score. Latent surprise (negative log-likelihood) is:

$$
  \ell_\theta(z) = -\log R_\theta(z).
$$

This first version implements latent density learning. Interpreting it as a
component of a biological world model remains a hypothesis.

### Measuring information

Mutual information measures how much the latent representation tells us about
sensory input. Expected KL divergence---a measure of difference between
distributions---provides an upper bound on this information rate.

Under the joint distribution $p(x)F(z \mid x)$, the aggregate latent
distribution is:

$$
  q_F(z) = \int p(x)F(z \mid x)\,dx.
$$

The variational rate identity underlying @alemi2018 gives:

$$
  \mathcal C(F,\theta)
  = \mathbb E_X D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(F(\cdot \mid X)\Vert R_\theta\big)
$$

$$
  \mathcal C(F,\theta) = I_F(X;Z) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q_F\Vert R_\theta\big)
                       \ge I_F(X;Z).
$$

**Interpretation:** expected KL equals information rate plus prior mismatch. For
fixed $F$ and $p(x)$, an unrestricted optimal prior matches $q_F$ and makes the
bound tight. A restricted learned prior may leave a positive gap.

Learning $R_\theta$ reduces prior mismatch, not the information retained by a
fixed encoder under a fixed input distribution. Improved coding efficiency is
the proposed biological interpretation; actual savings require a mechanism that
exploits the learned distribution. The bound alone does not establish such a
mechanism in organisms.

### Capacity constraint and complexity penalty

**Visual example:** [Rate--distortion and prior
mismatch](rate-distortion-prior.qmd) shows how learning the prior closes a KL
gap above a rate--distortion curve while holding the encoder fixed.

Suppose the information rate is bounded by capacity $K$:

$$
  I_F(X;Z) \le K.
$$

Imposing the tractable variational bound $\mathcal C(F,\theta) \le K$ is
sufficient to respect that capacity limit, but it can be conservative when the
prior is mismatched. For a fixed encoder and input distribution, improving the
prior fit lowers $\mathcal C(F,\theta)$ toward $I_F(X;Z)$ without changing the
information rate itself. Controlling code complexity through $\mathcal C$
therefore motivates learning an accurate perceptual prior $R_\theta$ alongside
or after acquiring $F$.

**Technical conditions:** finite KL requires appropriate prior support and a
well-defined rate; base-2 logs yield bits and natural logs yield nats. For
continuous representations, deterministic encoders may require noise or
quantization to obtain a finite information rate.

### Isolating prior learning with a fixed encoder

When training $F$ and $R_\theta$ jointly (as in $\mathcal D + \beta \mathcal C$),
updates to $F$ change the latent distribution $q_F$ that the prior must match.
To study prior learning on its own, assume $F$ has already learned useful
representations on a task, freeze its parameters (a stop-gradient equivalent),
and train only $R_\theta$. Freezing $F$ prevents encoder collapse during this
phase: the prior cannot reduce $\mathcal C$ by making $F$ discard distinctions.

For a fixed input distribution, prior learning then reduces only the mismatch
term $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_F\Vert R_\theta)$ while $I_F(X;Z)$ remains fixed.
Because changing which stimuli are attended changes the input distribution
$p(x)$, updating $R_\theta$ from trajectories collected under a different policy
requires correcting for that distribution shift back to the target policy. How an
agent might optimize a behavioral policy to sample trajectories for learning
$R_\theta$ is the subject of the [computational model of
aesthetics](computational-aesthetics.qmd).

### Future extension: temporal conditioning

The POMDP policy already uses memory $h_t$. A future extension would also
condition the encoder and perceptual prior on that memory:

$$
  F(z_t \mid x_t,h_t),\qquad R_\theta(z_t \mid h_t).
$$

The information-rate formulation would then use $I_F(X;Z \mid H)$, with a
corresponding conditional prior-mismatch term. This could capture sequence
expectations and order effects, though it is not required for the first version;
context choice and its availability to encoding and decoding processes would
need to be specified.

@lai2025 provide behavioral evidence for conditional policy compression,
measuring state-to-action information $I(S_t;A_t \mid S_{t-1})$. Applying that
principle to a perceptual channel is a proposed extension, not direct evidence
for a perceptual capacity bound. A separate action-policy complexity penalty is
not currently part of the model.

## Open questions

- **Encoder training:** which training stimuli, likelihood, architecture, and
  compression weight $\beta$ preserve distinctions useful for downstream
  decisions?
- **Objective weighting:** how should capacity constraints, complexity cost, and
  task performance be combined and weighted?
- **Perceptual prior family:** which normalized density family captures the
  regularities organisms learn?
- **Temporal extension:** when should the encoder and perceptual prior also
  condition on memory $h_t$, and what information should that memory contain?
